blogs.title: Distinguishing 'Right-to-Control' from 'Fraudulent Inducement' in the Wake of Ciminelli
blogs.description: This post analyzes how the Fifth Circuit navigated the Supreme Court’s recent narrowing of fraud statutes in Ciminelli v. United States. It explores the critical doctrinal distinction the court made between the 'right-to-control' theory (deprivation of information) and the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory (inducing a transaction). The post will discuss the implications for federal prosecutors who must now precisely tailor indicticts to ensure they allege a traditional property interest rather than mere economic disadvantage.

blogs.title: The 'Net Pecuniary Loss' Fallacy: How Kousisis Limits the Defense of Intent
blogs.description: Focusing on the court's application of Kousisis v. United States, this post examines the significant shift in the 'intent' element of securities fraud. It explores the court's reasoning that a defendant's intent to profit does not require a corresponding intent to cause a net economic loss to the victim. By analyzing the court’s 'distinction without a difference' approach, the post discusses why the mere transfer of property under false pretenses is sufficient for a fraud conviction, even if the victim ultimately holds a market-value asset.

blogs.title: Prosecuting the 'Finfluencer': Modernizing Fraud Theory for Social Media Schemes
blogs.description: This post takes a broader look at how the court’s interpretation of 18 U.S.C. § 1348 applies to the modern era of social media-driven 'pump and dump' schemes. It discusses the challenges of prosecuting influencers who leverage large followings to move markets and considers how the court's reliance on established mail and wire fraud concepts provides a robust framework for tackling decentralized, digital-first securities fraud.
